title: When To Praise Students So It Matters
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that indiscriminate, constant classroom praise -- what he compares to 'feeding ducks on a pond' -- is manipulative, dishonest, and corrosive to intrinsic motivation despite feeling kind in the moment. He offers a narrow, deliberately restrictive rule for when praise is warranted: only for genuinely new learning performed as taught, or for a true, sustained jump in performance or effort beyond a student's previous baseline, and never for routine expectations that have already become habitual. His reasoning is that praising ordinary compliance (pushing in a chair, lining up) puts it on the same level as a real breakthrough, like a strong essay or days of impeccable behavior, which cheapens both. He also weighs in on delivery, arguing that subtle, quiet acknowledgment -- eye contact, a nod, an understated comment -- is generally more effective than loud, effusive praise, because the student is already feeling their own accomplishment and the teacher is merely confirming it rather than manufacturing the feeling for them.
points: Restrict praise to two situations only: genuinely new learning performed as taught, and a true, sustained jump in performance or effort over the previous baseline.
Never praise routine, already-mastered expectations (pushing in a chair, lining up) -- doing so puts ordinary compliance on the same level as real breakthroughs.
Indiscriminate praise reads to students as manipulative and dishonest over time, undermining rather than building intrinsic motivation.
Favor quiet, understated acknowledgment (eye contact, a nod, a brief comment) over loud, effusive praise, since the student is already feeling the accomplishment themselves.
quotes: Common in this day and age is for teachers to throw out praise like they’re feeding ducks on a pond. A child does something/anything of the slightest value and they get a “good job!
Because indiscriminate praise is manipulative and dishonest and in the long run severely weakens intrinsic motivation. So when should you praise?
If a student or your class learns something for the first time, and performs it as taught, then you’re free to praise.
Once a routine or topic is learned, it becomes a common expectation and thus must not be praised.
It also places a true breakthrough—like a brilliantly written essay or several days of impeccable behavior—on the same level as pushing in a chair or lining up for lunch.
Eye contact and a nod of the head. A silent fist bump. An understated, “Now that’s how you do it.
